  • continuous employee development through the following ways

  • guidance.
  • Executive coaching helps leaders refine management and interpersonal skills.
  • Manage remote and virtual teams : The rise of remote work and online workforce
  • presents unique HRM challenges. Maintaining effective communication, collaboration
  • and performance management in a geographically dispersed workforce requires
  • innovative tools and strategies. Building trust and fostering a sense of team relation in a
  • virtual environment requires careful planning and constant effort.

  • 9 a) Narrate the HR Information System, its uses in HR Planning
  • HRIS is the application of Information Technology in the preparation and maintenance of HR
  • data. A HRIS is a software solution for organisations to automate HR management. HRIS
  • includes employees name, qualifications, date of birth, department, job title, date of joining
  • grade, salary, training completed and all the relevant data of the workforce. HRIS is typically
  • a database system that allows a company to track of all types of information related to HR.
  • HRIS combines in one system all the information that organisations typically keep on
  • workforce and positions. It can be formed by combing all HR data of an organisation in to
  • one database.
  • The effectiveness of HRP depends on the effectiveness of HRIS in that organisation because
  • HRP process work on the HR information supplied by the organisation. Past and present
  • information are necessary to predict future HR requirements.
  • Uses of HRIS in Human Resource Planning (HRP) (10marks)
  • A Human Resource Information System (HRIS) is a technology -based system that collects
  • stores, and processes HR data to support strategic and operational HR functions. In the
  • context of Human Resource Planning (HRP), HRIS is indispensable for ensuring that the
  • organisation has the right number of employees with the right skills at the right time. The
  • uses can be as follows
  • a) Workforce Data Management
  • b) Forecasting and demand supply analysis
  • c) Recruitment and staffing planning
  • d) Succession and career planning
  • e) Training and development planning
  • f) Performance management and decision support
  • e) Cost and budgeting control
  • f) Enhancing HR efficiency and accuracy
  • HRIS is a strategic tool for HRP , helping organisations forecast workforce needs, plan
  • recruitment and training, support succession, and make informed, cost -effective decisions.
  • By integrating data and analytics, HRIS ensures the right talent is available at the right time
  • enhancing organisational efficiency and competitiveness.

questions.question: Help the organization to come out from this critical issue. If you are in the role of HR manager what will be your immediate step to solve this case.
questions.solution_html:
• Growing Employee Expectations: Employee expectations and attitudes are changing.
  • Traditional inducements such as job security, compensation, housing and the like do not
  • attract and motivate today’s workforce.
  • (any 5 points)
  • 7 a. Analyse the impact of an ineffective performance appraisal system on employee
  • morale and organisational productivity
  • Performance appraisal is the periodical, formal evaluation of employee performance for
  • making career decisions. The absence of a reliable performance appraisal system will
  • deteriorate the whole process of HRM, resulting in the total waste of the valuable human
  • assets owned by the company. When implemented effectively, it motivates employees
  • aligns individual goals with organisational objectives, and enhances productivity.
  • However, an ineffective appraisal system one that is biased, inconsistent, or poorly
  • communicated can have serious negative consequences on both employee morale and
  • organisational productivity.
  • The impact of an ineffective performance appraisal system on employee morale and
  • organisational productivity are as follows
  • Reduced Job Satisfaction and Engagement- An ineffective appraisal system often
  • fails to provide constructive feedback or clear guidance for improvement.
  • Employees may not understand what is expected of them or how they can grow
  • within the organization, leading to frustration and disengagement.
  • Loss of Motivation and Engagement - If employees perceive the appraisal process
  • as unfair or inaccurate, they lose motivation to perform well. When high
  • performers receive the same ratings as low performers, it discourages effort and
  • fosters complacency.
  • Decline in Employee Retention - Talented employees are more likely to leave
  • when they feel their contributions are not recognised or fairly evaluated. This will
  • lead to high turnover rates and loss of organisational knowledge.
  • Perception of Bias and Favouritism - Subjective or poorly designed appraisal
  • systems often reflect personal bias rather than objective performance. Employees
  • may feel undervalued or discriminated against, leading to frustration, mistrust
  • and decreased job satisfaction.
  • Increased Stress and Anxiety - When appraisals focus solely on criticism without
  • constructive feedback, employees experience anxiety and job insecurity. This
  • will lead to Reduced confidence, increased absenteeism, and potential burnout
  • etc
  • An ineffective performance appraisal system can severely damage employee morale and
  • reduce organisational productivity. To prevent this, HRM must ensure objectivity
  • transparency, regular feedback, and developmental focus in the appraisal process. A fair and
  • constructive system transforms appraisals from a formality into a strategic tool for motivation
  • and growth.
  • (Any 5 points or other relevant points may be considered)
  • 7 b) Evaluate how basic salary and wages affect employee retention and turnover rates
  • in organisations, which system contribute more positively to employee loyalty?
  • Compensation is one of the strongest determinants of employee satisfaction and retention.
  • Basic salary and wages serve as the foundation of an employee’s financial security and
  • perception of fairness. When managed effectively, they enhance loyalty, reduce turnover, and
  • strengthen organisational commitment. However, i f poorly structured, they can lead to
  • dissatisfaction and high attrition rates.
  • Impact of Basic Salary on Employee Retention are (1.5marks)
  • a) Stability and Predictability
  • A basic salary provides employees with a consistent, predictable income. Financial stability
  • allows employees to focus on their work rather than personal financial stress. Result will be
  • increased job satisfaction and long-term commitment.
  • b) Perception of Fairness and Value
  • Employees view a fair salary as recognition of their contribution. This Enhances morale
  • motivation, and the psychological contract between employer and employee. This will reduce
  • the likelihood of seeking alternative employment.
  • c) Career Growth and Internal Equity
  • When basic salary structures reflect seniority, experience, and performance, employees
  • perceive growth opportunities within the organisation.
  • Impact of Wages on Retention and Turnover are (1.5marks)
  • a) Flexibility and Short-Term Motivation
  • Wages (often hourly or performance-based pay) can motivate short -term effort, particularly
  • in blue-collar or temporary jobs. This may encourage productivity but may not guarantee
  • long-term attachment.
  • b. Income Insecurity
  • Hourly or variable wage systems can create uncertainty when work hours fluctuate.
  • Employees may leave for more stable, salaried roles, increasing turnover rates.
  • c. Limited Career Attachment
  • Wage-based roles often lack progression frameworks, reducing employees’ sense of
  • belonging. Impact will be higher turnover, especially if better -paying options are available
  • elsewhere.
  • Evaluation: (2marks)
  • The basic salary system contributes more positively to employee loyalty and retention
  • because it offers financial stability, fairness, and a sense of belonging. In contrast, a wage
  • system may drive performance in the short term but fails to foster long -term commitment
  • especially where workers seek job security and career growth.
  • 8 a) Imagine you are an HR manager in a retail chain. How would you design a training
  • programme to improve emotional intelligence among frontline staff?
  • As an HR manager in a retail chain, design of a training programme would be to develop
  • emotional intelligence (EI) among frontline staff to improve customer service, teamwork, and
  • job satisfaction.
  • The first step would be to conduct a training needs analysis through employee feedback and
  • customer service reports to identify emotional or behavioural gaps. The programme’s key
  • objectives would be to enhance self -awareness, self -regulation, motivation, empathy, and
  • social skills—the five core elements of EI.
  • The training would include interactive workshops, role plays, and case studies that simulate
  • real customer interactions. Activities would focus on recognising emotions, managing stress
  • showing empathy towards customers, and communicating effectively with colleagues.
  • To reinforce learning, short follow -up sessions and coaching would be conducted monthly.
  • Evaluation would be based on improvements in customer satisfaction, peer feedback, and
  • observed behavioural changes.
  • Overall, this EI training programme would help staff handle customers more effectively, build
  • stronger team relationships, and create a positive retail environment that enhances both
  • employee morale and organisational performance.

questions.question: a. Case Study 1: Unilever's Global Virtual Team for Sustainable Innovation Background: Unilever, a global FMCG giant, has committed to achieving sustainability goals by 2030. To drive this initiative, the company formed a virtual innovation team consisting of employees from its R&D, marketing, and supply chain departments across the UK, India, Brazil, and the Netherlands. The team was tasked with designing eco-friendly packaging solutions. The team collaborated using platforms like Microsoft Teams, Trello, and cloud-based simulation tools. Members worked asynchronously due to time zone differences. Although the project progressed well, some issues emerged—cultural misunderstandings, uneven participation, and a lack of emotional connection among team members. The Turning Point: To address the issues, Unilever introduced structured "virtual bonding" sessions, digital brainstorming rooms, and a rotation system for team leads. With clear guidelines and regular feedback loops, the virtual team succeeded in developing a biodegradable packaging model within nine months—now implemented in over 30 countries.
